Abstract—The scientiﬁc literature on games and health ap-
plications aimed at helping decision-making for prostate cancer
is relatively modest, therefore, still requiring more signiﬁcant
contribution and exploration. This work presents a prostate can-
cer game based on decision-making and planning skills designed
to replicate classic real-world prostate symptoms, treatment
patterns, and care pathways. Players on the role of medical
professionals have to manage the patients’ health and cope with
the care of multiple prostate cancer patients concurrently. Which
patient to help ﬁrst and which medical tests to request to decide
the diagnosis and correct medical action are tasks that the player
has to manage. Since every decision has its consequences, the
ultimate goal is to make decisions without losing patients’ lives.
Index Terms—prostate cancer, interactive game, decision-
making, choices & consequences, planning skills
I. INTRODUCTION
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancer types
among men [1]. More speciﬁcally, the second and fourth
most commonly occurring, respectively, in men and overall.
About one man in eight will be diagnosed with prostate cancer
during his lifetime. It develops when abnormal cells multiply
and accumulate to form a tumor which can be cancerous or
benign. In more detail, prostate cancer affects the prostate
gland, located in the lower part of the male abdomen, just
below the bladder, and in front of the rectum [2].
Worldwide, about 75% of prostate cancer cases occur from
the age of 65. Some of these tumors can proliferate, spread
to other organs, and even lead to death. Most tumors evolve
slowly (it takes about 15 years to reach 1cm³), not becoming
an immediate threat to man’s health. Anyway, early diagnosis
is essential to maximize the likelihood of cure, and the harm
that this disease can cause to the individual’s health should not
be neglected [2]. Recently, according to the American Cancer
Society, the number of men who will die from prostate cancer
will hit a record high over the last two decades [3].

In parallel with that, computer games can create active
learning platforms applied to the health area [4]. Instead of
a didactic presentation that requires memorization or assimi-
lation of facts out of context, games promote situated learning
in which players can discover and learn through exploration
and experimentation. When playing a game, players can
cause desirable and undesirable health consequences through
decision-making without putting actual patients in danger. In
addition, games can help players make meaningful connections
between real-life and simulated events, thereby increasing the
likelihood that knowledge and skills experienced in the game
world are retained and applied in the real world.
Some authors discuss the beneﬁts and the importance of
developing more games aimed at the health care area, mainly
in Oncology [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Those authors present several
reasons explaining why computer games may provide beneﬁts,
for example: for doctors, by helping to improve the man-
agement of patient care; for medical institutions, by reducing
treatment costs and increasing the satisfaction of patients and
health professionals; for the Ministry of Health, by health
promotion through education; for society, by increasing the
level of participation in social activities through the learning
of social skills; and for patients, by promoting continuity of
care without the time and place restrictions.
The scientiﬁc literature on games and health applications
aimed at helping the decision-making for prostate cancer is
relatively modest [10], thus, still requiring greater contri-
bution and exploration. This work presents CancerSP (Fig.
1), a prototype game based on decision-making designed
to replicate classic real-world prostate symptoms, treatment
patterns, and care pathways. Players on the role of medical
professionals (Urologists, Oncologists, and Medical students)
have to manage the patients’ health and cope with the care of
multiple prostate cancer patients concurrently. Which patient
to help ﬁrst and which medical tests to request to decide the
diagnosis and correct medical action are tasks that the player

has to manage in this game. Since every decision has its
consequences, the ultimate goal is to make decisions without
losing patients’ lives. Having a game experience for decision-
making within the prostate cancer context may help medical
professionals and students practice prioritization in choosing
the right actions in the correct order and time, aiding in making
the best decisions for patients.
Fig. 1. Start screen of CancerSP game.
II. RELATED WORK
This section presents related work focused on serious games
and mobile phone applications developed to increase prostate
cancer awareness.
A. Serious Games
From simulated experiences on the common impacts on
patients’ quality of life with prostate cancer, the Time After
Time game [6] focuses on guiding players to choose the most
accepted cancer treatment strategy, considering the various
side effects it may cause. The side effects addressed in
the game relate to the following cancer treatments: radical
prostatectomy, brachytherapy, external radiation therapy, and
watchful waiting. The game show cards with examples of
side effects so that the user can classify them on a 5-point
scale (in which one means “without problems” and ﬁve means
“with major problems”). The ﬁrst round ends when the player
ﬁnishes sorting the side effect cards for all treatments and
periods. In the end, the player can view the result of the game,
which includes the cancer treatments with the side effects that
best meet the user’s preferences (in a way, empowering the
player) and a list of questions created for the doctor containing
doubts about the side effects found in the cards.
The Prostate Cancer Evaluation and Education game [7]
has been designed in collaboration with its target audience
towards increasing awareness of prostate cancer among Afro-
Caribbean men and encouraging symptomatic men to seek
medical help. In practice, this game features eight levels. In
seven of these levels, the user is presented with an infor-
mational area on how to play and with directed questions
about the assessment of the risk of prostate cancer, patient
concerns, family history, digital rectal examination (DRE),
urinary complaints, and prostate-speciﬁc antigen levels (PSA).
The last game level is used to evaluate the user’s responses
and encourages the patient to do an active search for medical
follow-up.
B. Mobile Phone Applications
The authors of a systematic review [10] of mobile phone
apps for quality of life and well-being assessment, especially
in prostate cancer patients, argue that people with cancer
tend to be more open to strategies that positively inﬂuence
their therapeutic process. Moreover, they suggest that game
developer should take special care in playtesting with this
audience and implement approaches more patient-centered.
WebChoice is a digital tool that has been developed in
cooperation between users and healthcare professionals [11]. It
contains tabs for recording symptoms and problems, sending
messages, writing a personal diary, opening public forums,
accessing bibliographies on each health issue, and oncology
nurses and doctors counseling. Studies conducted using this
tool have shown that men with prostate cancer have low
levels of social support and high levels of suffering due to
the symptoms of this disease, suggesting that these users may
ﬁnd such types of tools particularly useful.
Interaktor is an application for smartphones and tablets
developed to support the management symptoms of patients
with various types of cancer, including prostate cancer [12].
Concepts of participative and individual-centered care inspired
the development of the intervention. It includes four generic
components: (1) Self-assessment, (2) A risk assessment model,
(3) Evidence-based self-care advice & links to relevant web
pages, and (4) Graphs showing the history of symptoms re-
ported to patients and healthcare professionals. Authors report
that the application promoted the patient’s participation in their
care through continuous and convenient contact with health
professionals.
A slightly different approach to assess the usability and
patient experience is presented in [13], with a mHealth appli-
cation named myPROHealth. This application focuses on men
who are about to start androgen deprivation therapy, i.e., a ther-
apy that increases the risk of adverse metabolic effects among
patients with prostate cancer. The application’s features allow
patients to enter information about their physical activity and
recent meals and monitor their treatment evolution. Although
the number of users who participated in the user tests was
minimal (only ﬁve patients, with an average age of 62 years,
and ﬁve doctors), the results from the qualitative assessments
revealed that patients, in general, valued the holistic care
provided by the application.
These works use different initiatives, such as guiding users
to choose the most accepted strategy of prostate cancer treat-
ment, supporting the management symptoms of patients with
cancer, among others. However, the remaining gap is the lack
of previous prostate cancer games based on decision-making
and planning skills. This work ﬁlls a gap by designing a
prostate cancer game that focuses on decision-making, and
classic real-world prostate symptoms, treatment patterns, and
care pathways. Finally, while management games let players

manage every aspect of a person’s life, this work aims to
mix decision-making with managing multiple patients with
potential prostate cancer concurrently. From managing time
with various patients to handling complicated patient care
situations, players can expect to experience problems related
to what action they should do ﬁrst using planning skills. In our
game, patients’ symptoms and family medical history provide
the initial information for recognizing what medical actions
must come ﬁrst to identify priority clinical case scenarios for
making better treatment decisions.
III. GENERAL DESCRIPTION
Prostate cancer is usually diagnosed by prostate biopsy
prompted by a blood test to measure PSA and/or DRE [14].
PSA is a protein produced by normal, as well as malignant,
cells of the prostate gland. DRE involves a doctor feeling the
prostate through the wall of the back passage (rectum) to verify
if one has a prostate problem or prostate cancer.
Symptoms fundamentally depend on the location and extent
of the disease. Most cases are diagnosed by screening and,
thus, patients, in general, have no suspicious symptoms of the
disease. In case of a possible localized cancer disease, the most
common symptoms originate from the lower urinary tract,
showing dysuria (pain when urinating), increased urination,
hesitation, and reduced urinary jet, erectile dysfunction, etc.
[2]. Cases of locally advanced disease can present hema-
turia (blood in the urine), urinary retention, pelvic pain, and
hematospermia (blood in the sperm). On the other hand, in
cases of advanced disease, the patient’s symptomatology will
depend on the location of the metastasis.
Most prostate cancers are diagnosed after a PSA elevated
for age and/or prostatic nodule detected in DRE, being per-
formed transrectal prostate biopsy by ultrasound. Patients
with metastatic disease have signiﬁcantly elevated PSA and
can obtain histological evidence for diagnosis by biopsy or
site of metastatic disease. After conﬁrming the diagnosis of
prostate cancer, an evaluation should be carried out through
laboratory tests and imaging exams to stage the disease and
plan treatment. The imaging tests to be ordered will depend
on the clinical presentation of each patient and each risk of
cancer stratiﬁcation [14].
The Gleason score [15] is a score given to prostate cancer
based on its microscopic appearance. It is important because
higher scores are associated with a worse prognosis. In terms
of local staging, magnetic resonance imaging has often been
used since it allows a better correlation with the volume of the
cancer disease. In addition, another potential advantages are
the staging of the primary tumor, which can assist in cancer
treatment in some cases.
To ﬁght against prostate cancer and, consequently, save
lives, through the exercise of clinical diagnosis, decision
making, and cancer treatment, the player must manage the
following resources available in the Game home interface:
• Medical Tests, Imaging and Interventions: PSA (or
Blood Test) & DRE (or Touch Test), Ultrasound (US) &
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Biopsy.
• Medical Treatments: Based on the results obtained from
PSA, DRE, US, MRI, and Biopsy, one can apply one
or more treatments appropriate to the prostate cancer
type, such as Radiotherapy, Surgery, Chemotherapy, and
Hormone therapy.
Clinical Reasoning is an important aspect of health profes-
sional education and practice [16]. The basics and fundamen-
tals, when put together, reﬂect a physician’s ability to make
decisions and diagnoses. Depending on the results obtained
from the medical tests, imaging, interventions, and patient’s
age, family medical history, and symptoms, a decision has to
be made.
IV. ART & DESIGN
The design of this game was conceived by one of the authors
of this work. The game art was developed as a collection of
image sprites and icons, most of them created by the authors,
and some others owned by third parties offered through the
Website [17], [18]. The light blue ribbon as a symbol of
prostate cancer awareness was our inspiration to choose the
color palette and create the art of our game as an emblem of
the prostate cause.
In our game, the player takes on the role of saving patients
with suspected prostate cancer. The music sets the tone for the
importance of medical care [19]. So, we opted for creating a
Start screen still, with a near-dead silent and a simple menu
(Fig. 1), which includes the following options: Start, Setup,
Credits, and Exit. After starting the game, the melody bounces
according to the player’s initiatives in saving patients’ lives or
when losing lives [20]. The musical theme sets the tone for
what is to come during gameplay.
The decisions of images and sounds joined on the game
screens were made considering how both aspects continually
inﬂuenced each other, mainly focused on the decision-making
and consequences context, when trying to save the lives of pa-
tients with different types of prostate symptoms concurrently.
The sound also provides feedback and alerts for the player,
including button-press clicks, signs, etc.
In this prototype version of the game, we modeled 18 classic
clinical case scenarios in the context of prostate cancer to
put player’s diagnostic, management, and treatment skills to
the test. We describe these case scenarios as follows: healthy
prostate, prostate with painful condition (with different levels
of pain), prostate bleeding (with the small, medium, and large
bloody ﬂow), prostate with varying sizes of tumor and stages
of development, prostate with inﬂammation, and prostate with
different types of metastasis, as shown in Fig.2.
In the upper panel of the Game home screen, there are
different clinical cases of patients presented simultaneously (in
Fig. 3, Fred, Peter, and Sam), being three at a time. That is,
multiple clinical case scenarios are dynamically spawned on
the Game home screen. The player must manage the patients’
health as quickly and precisely as possible. Every decision has
its consequences, so the ultimate goal is to make decisions
without losing the patients’ lives.

To help in the decision-making process, the initial data input
for each patient is presented to the player on the top of the
Game home panel, in each patient’s lane, as follows: Name
(names are ﬁctional), Age, Symptoms, and Family Medical
History. The player can scroll the panel down to facilitate
the reading and monitoring of all clinical cases.
Icons are an essential part of game user interfaces, visually
expressing objects and actions. We use icons on the six
buttons displayed in the lower area of the Game home screen
(Fig. 3) to control game mechanics. More speciﬁcally, Figs.
4.a, b, c, d, e, and f detail the game features available to
the player for clinical diagnosis, intervention, and treatment:

Medical tests (PSA & DRE) and imaging (US & MRI),
intervention (Biopsy), and treatments (Radiotherapy, Surgery,
Chemotherapy, and Hormone therapy). As the player interacts
with the game environment using these action buttons, updated
information about the clinical case scenarios is displayed on
each patient’s lane.
There is a return icon on the top left side of the Game home
screen to make it possible to go back to the Start screen. On the
right side of the return icon, ﬁve heart icons show how many
life points the player begins the game with. In other words,
how many times can the player make wrong decisions to the
end of losing all the patient’s lives before being eliminated
from play (game over). There is a menu icon on the top right
side of the Game home screen with the following options:
Help, Restart, and Exit.
V. GAME DEVELOPMENT
CancerSP is a computer game made using Unity [21],
currently still the most popular platform to build games with.

With multiple patients to care concurrently (each one in a
different lane), the player needs to be more detached to activate
and manage multiple game elements simultaneously. The
diagram shown in Fig. 5 is a general ﬂowchart representing the
ﬂow of the prostate cancer game from start to ﬁnish. According
to the player’s actions, each patient’s health status can improve
or worsen during gameplay. Thus, to select and take care of
any patient, the player must ﬁrst click on a particular dynamic
patient’s sprite (Fig. 3) to activate the diagnosis and treatment
options. Currently, the clinical cases are hardwired in-game
logic. The static clinical cases contain the patient information
and the order of operations necessary to consider the patient
as “cured”.
Illustrative Example: The following patient’s clinical case
scenario is shown in the middle lane of Fig. 3: a 73-year-
old man named Peter Parker reported having hematuria, with
a family medical history of prostate cancer (father). His past
medical history was unremarkable. To investigate this clinical
case, the player must ﬁrst select the patient by clicking on
his name (Peter) on the blue label at the top of the patient’s
sprite. A similar procedure must be done to interact with the
other two patient cases, selecting any of their names: Fred or
Sam. By pressing the PSA & DRE button icon (Fig. 4.a),
a PSA level 10 ng/mL is shown in the top panel of the
Game home screen. And, when scrolling down (the player
can scroll down the panel content wherever necessary), the
DRE revealed a slightly enlarged and signiﬁcant asymmetry
prostate. By asking for a prostatic biopsy (Fig. 4.b), the player
is notiﬁed that the biopsy result was positive for malignancy
in both lobes, clinical stage T2, and revealed a Gleason score
of 7 (4 + 3) adenocarcinoma. Based on this information, the
player can make a treatment decision, that is, for this case
report, to undergo surgery (radical prostatectomy) (Fig. 4.e),
followed by Hormone therapy (Fig. 4.f).
Basically, from the player perspective, the patient’s choice
criteria will most likely be based on the severity of his health
status (the closer the patient’s sprite is to the end of the
lane, the higher the risk of patient’s health, requiring priority
emergency care). As time goes by, the game dynamics are as
follows: all the “patients” will fall vertically in an animation
movement of translation. When the patient reaches the base of
the Game home screen, there are two options: either the player
will save the patient’s life or lose it. In the latter case, at the
top of the Game home screen, one life point (heart icon) will
be removed for each life lost.
If the player makes a wrong decision, this causes the player
to lose one of the ﬁve life points. As a result, one life
point is taken away from the Game home screen. The game
continues, and the player starts again will all the remaining
lives. Likewise, if the player makes a wrong medical decision,
this decreases the patient’s life and may cost another life point.
The game continues like this until there are no more life
points available (i.e., the player lost ﬁve patients’ lives) or until
the player completes the game (i.e., the player saved many
patients’ lives and lost less than ﬁve life points). If the player
succeeds in completing the gameplay, a victory is achieved,
as shown in Fig. 6. Otherwise, a message is shown regretting
the loss of patients’ lives (Figs. 7 and 8).
Other essential elements in the game appear when the game
is over. The game ends when the clinical case scenarios pre-
sented in-game are over, and the player successfully managed
to save the majority of patient’s lives, or when ﬁve life points

A. Animations
Most of the animations are used when the patient’s state
changes. In groups of three, sprite images representing differ-
ent clinical case scenarios of patients with prostate symptoms
are moved down vertically, representing their respective life
journeys. The player must be aware that the health of the three
patients needs to be managed simultaneously. We designed this
type of game interaction to create a more engaging experience
by motivating players to get better and faster at making
decisions, similar to actual Hospital-Based Emergency Care.
In patients with prostate cancer, the disease can evolve or
involute, depending on the player’s actions. Given the clinical
scenario of each patient, every time the player makes the
correct decision, the patient gains lifetime (his sprite goes
up, instead of falling down the lane). On the other hand,
when the player makes a wrong decision, the patient loses
his lifetime (his sprite falls faster). When a patient is near
the end of his lane, we scale his sprite down so that he
can cross the quadrilateral object located between the action
buttons and leave the Game home screen, representing a gate
metaphorically to the life or death.
To represent these changes in the patients’ clinical condition
and provide the player with a more engaging and interactive
experience, we designed and implemented different animations
focused on cancer symptoms using sprite animations. The
sprite animations were created using keyframe animation in
Unity. Unity interpolates the data from one keyframe to the
next to play the animation when the animation plays. Among
the collection of sprites (Fig. 2) we have designed for the
animations, the classic prostate symptoms implemented in this
version of the game using animations were the following:
• Prostate with pain: Represented by a throbbing visual
effect. By improving this symptom, this visual effect is
turned off;
• Prostate with hematuria: Represented by three sprites
with incremental intensities of bleeding. By improving
this symptom, the same animation approach is used,
however, in the reverse order of keyframes;
• Prostates with tumors that increase in size, number,
and/or undergo metastasis over time: Represented
by sprites with three incremental levels of tumor size,
number of tumors, and types of metastasis.
Finally, through Events in Unity, visual effects start and stop
spawning particles periodically using a time delay, as shown
in Fig. 6 in the form of light blue awareness ribbons scattered
around the phrase “Congratulations! Many lives were saved!”.
VI. PLAYTESTING
A. Participants
First, for having an initial measure of the perceived usability
of the game, we have conducted a playtesting session with
only one specialist user who detected the need to calibrate the

movement speed of the patients’ sprites to generate a better
game experience.
Initially, the time limit for saving each patient was the 30s.
This value proved to be unsuitable even for players who like
to play at a fast pace. It has generated a very high level
of difﬁculty and, more importantly, it failed to convey the
patient’s input data adequately and clearly. Thus, the time
limit was adjusted to 60s, which proved to be much more
compatible with the game’s goals without harming the sprite
animations and player interaction quality. It is important to
reinforce that, in addition to the challenge of controlling
multiple patients’ sprites at a time, there is also the challenge
of evaluating each clinical case scenario and be conﬁdent in
making the appropriate decision during gameplay by reading
and processing each medical information displayed on the
Game home screen.
Since a qualitative study with ﬁve users is likely to uncover
85% of the usability problems in a design [22], following that,
we conducted playtesting with a small sample of ﬁve users (3
males and two females). Overall, participants showed a similar
level of knowledge about prostate cancer. The goal was to
determine the main issues of our game prototype and ﬁx them.
B. Questionnaires
First, we began with the application of an online question-
naire using Google Meet to allow audio and visual commu-
nication between each participant and the facilitator, with the
following qualitative questions:
1) Did you like the game’s visual aesthetic?
2) Were the sound effects and musical theme appropriate
for the game?
3) Did you ﬁnd useful the learning design of the game?
4) Did you ﬁnd the prostate cancer cases representative?
5) Did you like the experience?
6) Would you have suggestions for game reﬁnement and
improving?
Then, we applied an online version of the SUS (System
Usability Scale) questionnaire, one of the best known and
simplest methods of verifying the usability of a “system” [23].
The SUS questionnaire consists of 10 questions, and for each
of them the user can answer on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1
means Completely Disagree and 5 means Completely Agree.
The questions are as follows:
1) I think I would like to use this game often.
2) I ﬁnd the game unnecessarily complex.
3) I found the game easy to use.
4) I think I would need help from a person with technical
knowledge to use the game.
5) I think the various functions of the game are very well
integrated.
6) I think the game has a lot of inconsistencies.
7) I imagine that people will learn how to use this game
quickly.
8) I found the game awkward to use.
9) I felt conﬁdent using the game.
10) I needed to learn a lot of new things before I was able
to use the game.
VII. RESULTS
As for comparison, the average SUS score is 68 [23]. In
this work, the raw SUS score was 76.5. When converted into
a percentile, the SUS score was 72.27, describing the game
experience as “Good”.
Regarding the qualitative testing with ﬁve participants, we
focused on the paths participants took to achieve their goals
in the game, what problems they had, and the comments they
made. The results from the qualitative assessments revealed
that some players clicked ﬁrst the Biopsy button instead of
the US & MRI one, even when the priority action was to
ask for an ultrasound. This problem probably was due to the
positioning of the Biopsy button on the Game home interface,
which is located to the left of the US & MRI button, as shown
in Fig. 3. The initiative to mitigate this problem when revising
the game will be to invert the positions of these two buttons.
All the participants liked the visual game’s aesthetics.
They reported that the multiple management of clinical case
scenarios was a very engaging experience, with comments
reinforcing how excited and emotionally touched they were,
respectively, during the winning (saving lives) and losing
moments (losing lives).
The participants very much appreciated the sound effects
and the musical theme. These audio elements helped to create
reﬂective moments and to provoke decision-making actions
demanding full player attention. They mentioned that ludic
game aspects help to give them agency. In addition, in gen-
eral, participants commented that the minimalist soundtrack
brought concentration and a more engaging and immersive
atmosphere.
Participants found representative the classic prostate cancer
scenarios presented in the game. Four participants (three males
and one female) expressed they had a meaningful interactive
experience. Moreover, they commented about how important
it is to focus on content related to the cancer condition to
promote men’s health.
Regarding the learning aspects of the game, participants
who had family members and close friends with prostate
cancer were able to make decisions more effectively. Perhaps
this happens because they have some familiarity with the
diagnostic process and/or with the medical tests commonly
requested (we will need additional playtesting with more
participants to clarify this issue). Two participants complained
about the small font size of the patient input data displayed
on the top panel of the Game home screen.
VIII. LIMITATIONS
Because the pandemic currently constrains human resources
and time, this study was limited to generating online knowl-
edge from the available participants. The study is also limited
to a small sample of participants. It does not necessarily
reﬂect other populations of users, such as people with no
knowledge about prostate cancer or, on the contrary, people

highly specialized in this subject. Anyway, how players en-
gaged in these prior experiences will indeed serve to enhance
gameplay design. Future research efforts may need to include
a representative number of Urologists, Oncologists, and Med-
ical students. Efforts should involve these potential players
to collect their feedback and use it for game revision and
reﬁnement to proceed from a prototype to a ﬁnal executable
game by polishing implementation details and adding custom
game improvements over time.
IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
A game is a form of interactive entertainment where players
must overcome challenges by taking actions governed by
rules to meet a victory condition [24]. In the health area,
the design of games that engage the audience and provide
a meaningful experience is a complex task. However, when
well designed, an interactive game can ease learning concepts
and skills in the medical ﬁeld, such as those related to prostate
cancer, by managing multiple clinical case scenarios concur-
rently using decision-making. Overall, preliminary ﬁndings
of players’ experiences and perceptions of our game were
very positive. During gameplay, the highly interactive nature
and ludic game elements helped to give participants agency.
Our ﬁndings also suggest that the gameplay’s visual, textual,
and audio elements may help increase the awareness and
the generation of meaningful experiences for players. These
experiences focus on the content of prostate cancer condition
and on choosing the right medical actions in the proper order
and time, without losing patients’ lives.
Future work would beneﬁt from using a data-driven ap-
proach to dynamically load many clinical cases of patients
with prostate cancer symptoms based on a state machine
that works on data containing their medical history and pre-
existing conditions. Another necessary extension of this work
is to create game levels with a purpose to amp up, even
more, the player experience. In particular, we highlight the
fundamental importance of heterogeneous team collaboration
in this work, especially medical professionals. Finally, we will
use the lessons learned with this preliminary usability study to
reﬁne the future versions of our prostate cancer game before
being shared with a broader audience. We also plan to test the
new revised versions of our game with specialized players in
the short future.
